newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: PRESS DIGEST-Australian General News - April 18.
newsitem.headline: PRESS DIGEST-Australian General News - April 18.

text.p: (Compiled for Reuters by Media Monitors)
THE AUSTRALIAN FINANCIAL REVIEW

Prime Minister John Howard has made some concessions to Aboriginal negotiators in the latest response to the High Court's Wik decision. The concessions include the possibility that sunset clauses for native title claims be dropped and that government legislation could include a provision for regional and local agreements. Page 3.

The federal government's planned superannuation surcharge for high income earners faces major amendments in the Senate. The move, planned to raise up to A$1.5 billion in revenue over three years, does not have the support of Tasmanian Independent Senator Brian Harradine who now commands the balance of power in the upper house. Page 3.

Australian Bureau of Statistics figures released yesterday reveal time lost to industrial disputes has climbed dramatically under the Howard government with an increase of almost 70 percent in the number of days lost to industrial disputes in 1996 compared with the previous year under a Labor administration. Page 4.

The latest survey of business conditions from the Metal Trades Industry Association highlights continuing problems in Australia's manufacturing sector with more than one-third of firms reporting falling activity levels and labour cutbacks during the March quarter. However, the figures also reveal high capital expenditure over the period as firms anticipate an improvement in market conditions later this year. Page 5.
THE AUSTRALIAN

Prime Minister John Howard's recent decision to reject the vote of embattled Senator Mal Colston has placed in jeopardy the government's planned tax on the superannuation of high income earners. Independent Senator Brian Harradine, who will now hold the Senate balance of power in his own right, has signalled his opposition to the A$500 million-a-year super tax, allowing Labor, the Democrats and Greens to strike important section of the controversial legislation. Page 1.

Pro-euthanasia campaigner Dr Philip Nitschke has admitted providing coma-inducing drugs to 56-year-old terminally ill woman who died four days into the coma. Esther Wild, who had pleaded in vain with the Senate for voluntary euthanasia, died early yesterday morning. Nitschke said he acted within the law, saying the drugs were administered at Wild's request to alleviate her pain. Page 1.

Steve Waugh has been picked as the Australian cricket team vice-captain on the Ashes tour. Waugh replaces wicket-keeper Ian Healy who was sacked from the deputy position. Embattled skipper Mark Taylor will remain captain when the team takes off for the upcoming English tour. Page 1.

The decision by major United States tobacco companies to seek a US$300 billion (A$390 billion) out-of-court settlement for health claims was labelled as a "significant moment" by the federal government last night. Health Minister Dr Michael Wooldridge said the government was seeking legal advice on whether a similar deal could be reached in Australia. Page 1.
THE SYDNEY MORNING HERALD

Australian health and anti-smoking groups have called on the federal government to launch a massive compensation claim against tobacco giants following an estimated A$400 billion deal in the United States. Federal Health Minister Dr Michael Wooldridge said health authorities were considering launching a U.S.-style litigation but the federal government had no plans to challenge the tobacco industry in court at this stage. Page 1.

The government is about to learn an alternate meaning to the term "star-struck". Oscar-winning actor Geoffrey Rush and directors Gillian Armstrong (Oscar and Lucinda), Chris Noonan (Babe) and Scott Hicks (Shine) are understood to have written to Prime Minister John Howard, protesting proposed cuts to the A$140 million federal assistance to the film industry. Page 1.

The Victorian Government has moved to sell the management of its entire public transport system. The A$190 million-a-year loss-making system will be the first in Australia to become completely privatised. Under the plan, the government will retain ownership of rolling stock, but management of the service is expected to be in private hands by late next year. Page 1.

The federal government has blamed the Opposition's refusal to accept the Senator Mal Colston vote-discount deal which may see controversial small business reforms - including the scrapping of unfair dismissal laws - rejected by the Senate. Independent Senator Brian Harradine now holds the pivotal Senate vote and he signalled last year that he did not support parts of the government's industrial relations reforms. Page 2.
THE AGE

Melbourne's trams, trains and buses will be sold-off by the Kennett government by December next year. The sale of the entire public transport system represents a major shift in the state government's election commitment which was limited to contracting out some maintenance and freight services and restructuring the system's corporate body, the Public Transport Corporation. Page 1.

A Government inquiry into allegations of abuse of state wards in Victoria during the 1950s and 1960s was welcomed by state ward operator the Sisters of Mercy religious order. Leader of the Sisters of Mercy's Melbourne congregation Sister Helen Delaney said the order wants the truth to come out - regardless of what it is. Page 1.

The grieving family of a boy killed by a pet dog has made an impassioned warning to others not to trust large dogs. A bull mastiff-great dane cross, a family pet, savaged and killed a 12-year-old boy in the backyard of his Melbourne home on Wednesday. The boy's brother said the dog had never displayed any behaviour which would indicate the tragedy. Page 1.

The Australian Broadcasting Corporation's Radio Australia network may be saved from the axe with the federal government referring the fate of the overseas broadcaster back to its expenditure review committee. The move reflects concern from senior government ministers including Alexander Downer, Deputy Prime Minister Tim Fischer and Government Senate Leader Senator Robert Hill. Page 3.
-- Reuters Sydney Newsroom 61-2 9373-1800
